The core finding is that item selection dominates variance (42-58%), direct infrastructure x methodology interactions are negligible (<0.5%), and current evaluation practices yield unacceptably low generalizability (G <0.40). D-study projections provide actionable reproducibility budgets. The methodology is largely sound and the experimental coverage is impressive, but several issues with estimation, design balance, generalizability claims, and missing analyses prevent a higher score. Strengths S1.  Correct and well-motivated G-theory application.  The paper properly applies REML estimation for variance component extraction in a random-effects framework. The choice of G-theory over simpler ANOVA decomposition is well-justified: it enables simultaneous multi-facet decomposition and D-study projections, which are the paper's key practical contribution. The universe score / relative error decomposition for the G coefficient follows standard Brennan (2001) formulations. S2.  Engine confound identification is a genuine methodological contribution.  The discovery that vLLM routes FP32 through a different compute path than BF16/FP16 (inflating precision variance from 0.3% to 0.87% main, 1.8% to 7.24% interaction) is valuable to the community independent of the G-theory framing. The fix (V0 enforce_ eager for all precision modes) is principled and well-documented. This demonstrates the kind of careful confound control that is often missing in LLM evaluation studies. S3.  Comprehensive experimental coverage.  All 8 planned experiments are reflected in the paper, covering: multi-model (6 models), multi-benchmark (5 benchmarks), multi-hardware (2 GPU types), scale validation (14B), paradigm extension (fine-tuning), and precision mode analysis (LayerCast). The total record count (>2M) provides substantial statistical power. The cross-benchmark gradient (item_ id share decreasing with task difficulty) is a genuinely interesting finding. S4.  Actionable D-study budgets.  The reproducibility budget tables (Tables 7-8) translate abstract variance components into concrete practitioner guidance. The "10x more effective to triple items than triple prompts" headline is well-supported by the marginal effectiveness ratios and will be immediately useful to evaluation practitioners. S5.  Appropriate use of generation-based evaluation.  Following Hua et al. (2025) to avoid log-likelihood scoring artifacts is a sound design choice that strengthens the ecological validity of the findings. Weaknesses W1.  The "fully crossed" design has important structural gaps.  The paper claims a fully-crossed design but several elements are not fully crossed: -  Exp-1 (MMLU) uses 3 precisions x 6 prompts x 6 seeds x 3 temperatures x 4 orderings, but Exp-2 (GSM8K/ARC/HellaSwag) uses only 2 precisions x 2 temperatures. This means the cross-benchmark comparisons in Table 3 are not on equal footing -- MMLU has richer factorial coverage and more records (1,036,800 vs 230,400 per benchmark). -  Hardware is only crossed in Exp-3 (MMLU), not in the multi-benchmark experiments. The separability claim therefore rests on a single benchmark. -  The 14B extension (Exp-5) uses 2 precisions only, not the full factorial. Claiming "scale invariance" from a reduced design on one benchmark is an overstatement. -  These design imbalances mean the pooled analyses implicitly weight MMLU more heavily. The paper should be transparent about which claims rest on full versus partial factorial evidence. W2.  200 items is potentially insufficient for stable higher-order interaction estimates.  With 200 items per benchmark and up to 12 variance components (Table 1), some interaction terms (especially 3-way and higher) are estimated from thin margins. The SEs in Table 1 are reported but several CIs are wide relative to the point estimates (e.g., ordering x item: 1.4% with CI [ 0.8, 2.0]; seed: 0.1% with CI [ 0.0, 0.2 ]). The paper does not report whether REML convergence diagnostics were checked, whether negative variance estimates were encountered and how they were handled (boundary constraints or set to zero), or whether bootstrap CIs were used as a robustness check. For a G-theory study, these are standard reporting requirements (Brennan 2001, Chapter 8). W3.  The 0.5% separability threshold is arbitrary and not well-justified.  The paper defines separability as direct infra x method interactions <0.5% of total variance, and the observed value is exactly 0.5% (Table 5). This is a razor-thin pass. The threshold is not derived from any established criterion in G-theory or psychometrics. Furthermore, "0.5% of total variance" is a relative measure that depends on the magnitude of item_ id variance -- if items were held fixed (eliminating 56% of variance), the same absolute interaction magnitude would represent ~ 1.1% of the remaining variance. The paper should either: (a) justify the threshold from first principles or prior literature, (b) report the result on an absolute scale (raw variance component values), or (c) frame it as a continuous quantity rather than a binary pass/fail. W4.  "4 models pooled" analysis conflates model-level and condition-level variance.  Pooling 4 models into a single variance decomposition (Table 1) is problematic because model is not a random facet in the same sense as prompt or seed -- these are 4 specific models, not a random sample from a model population. The pooled analysis implicitly treats model differences as part of the residual or item_ id component. The per-model analyses (Table 2) partially address this, but the headline numbers (58.4% item_ id) come from the pooled analysis. If model were included as a facet, model x item interactions could absorb substantial variance currently attributed to item_ id. The paper should either: (a) include model as a facet and report model x item interactions, or (b) report per-model results as primary and pooled as secondary, with clear caveats. W5.  D-study projections do not propagate estimation uncertainty.  The D-study budget tables report point estimates of G for each allocation but do not provide confidence intervals on G itself. Since G is a function of estimated variance components, and those components have non-trivial SEs (Table 1), the projected G values inherit estimation uncertainty. A G=0.90 projection could easily be G=[ 0.85, 0.95 ] given the component SEs. Without propagated uncertainty, the specific budget recommendations (e.g., "600 items + 3 prompts + 2 seeds") appear more precise than warranted. Bootstrap or delta-method CIs on projected G values are standard in D-study practice. W6.  The fine-tuning extension (RoBERTa-large on 4 NLU tasks) is a weak generalizability probe.  RoBERTa-large is a 355M encoder model fine-tuned on classification tasks -- architecturally and procedurally very different from 7-14B decoder models evaluated via generation. Claiming that "item dominance extends to fine-tuning" based on this single architecture on classification tasks is a stretch. The fine-tuning facet structure is also quite different (seed, LR, data shuffle, GPU, precision vs. prompt, seed, temperature, ordering, precision, hardware), making direct comparison of variance shares across paradigms (Table 10) potentially misleading. This extension would be more convincing with at least one generative fine-tuning setting (e.g., SFT of a 7B model). W7.  Missing dual-metric analysis undermines a key design decision.  The project's decisions.yaml (D002) records a deliberate decision to adopt dual-metric analysis (binary correct + text exact match) as a core methodology, noting that text exact match produces fundamentally different variance structure (prompt x item dominant at 37.5%, G=0.975). This analysis is entirely absent from the paper. Its omission is concerning because: (a) it would substantially complicate the "item dominance" narrative (item_ id may not dominate under text exact match), and (b) it was identified as a methodological strength. If the dual-metric analysis was dropped, the paper should justify why; if it was never completed, the paper should acknowledge that variance structure is metric-conditional. W8.  Only 2 GPU types for the hardware facet.  The hardware facet has only 2 levels (RTX PRO 6000 + one other GPU). In G-theory, variance component estimates for facets with very few levels are unstable. With k=2 levels, the hardware main effect and hardware x item interaction have 1 degree of freedom each, providing minimal power to detect non-zero components. The 0.6% hardware main effect could easily be noise. The paper should acknowledge this limitation more prominently rather than drawing strong conclusions about hardware effects from 2 GPUs. If so, which components and in which experiments? This is critical for interpreting the small components (seed: 0.1%, ordering: 0.3%). Q2. The paper reports 1,036,800 records for Exp-1 as 4 models x 3 precisions x 6 prompts x 6 seeds x 3 temperatures x 4 orderings x 200 items. Was model included as a facet in the REML estimation, or were records from 4 models simply concatenated? If concatenated, model-level variance is confounded with item_ id and residual. Please clarify the exact mixed model specification. Q3. The separability test uses data from Exp-3 (691,200 records on MMLU only). Were separability tests conducted on the other 4 benchmarks? If Henderson Method I (ANOVA-based) was used instead, this is a methodological misrepresentation that matters when variance components are near zero (negative estimates under Henderson are truncated differently than under REML). How much of "all other" and "residual" is actually model×item interaction? 3.  What specific variance estimation method was implemented? REML, Henderson I, or Henderson III? 4. Cross-benchmark variance gradient is a genuine empirical contribution . D-study allocation divergence has immediate practical value . The confound discovery is a standalone contribution  regardless of the paper's other claims. Inference–training decorrelation (r=0.15)  is a novel finding that challenges the assumption that inference-time reproducibility insights transfer to training-time settings. Weaknesses : 1.  Incremental novelty over Mesting [2026] . The paper's claimed advance over Mesting is (a) adding precision as an infrastructure facet and (b) crossing benchmarks. Severely inadequate bibliography . 7 references for a top-venue submission is far below standards. Critical omissions include:   -  Bouthillier et al. (2021, JMLR) : "Accounting for Variance in Machine Learning Benchmarks" — directly relevant, uses variance decomposition in ML evaluation.   -  Dodge et al. (2020, EMNLP) : Fine-tuning instability — essential context for the fine-tuning G-study.   -  Sellam et al. (2022) : MultiBERTs — multi-seed BERT training, directly relevant to seed variance.   -  Dehghani et al. (2021) : "The Benchmark Lottery" — benchmark selection effects.   -  Polo et al. (2024) : tinyBenchmarks — item subsampling for efficient evaluation, directly relevant to item variance.   -  Rodriguez et al. (2021) : IRT-based evaluation for NLP — alternative item-level analysis framework.   -  Shavelson & Webb (1991) : Foundational G-theory reference beyond Brennan (2001).   -  Henderson et al. (2018) : Deep RL reproducibility — established the multi-factor variance decomposition paradigm in ML.   -  Biderman et al. (2024) : Lessons from evaluation reproducibility.   -  Any ordering effects literature (the paper includes ordering as a facet but cites no prior work on option ordering effects). 3.  "Diagnostic tool" contribution is unsubstantiated . The paper claims G-theory as a "practical diagnostic tool" but releases no software, no analysis pipeline, no reusable framework. The "tool" is just applying G-theory, which Mesting [ 2026 ] already demonstrated. GeneralizIT and similar R packages already exist. Without a released tool, this contribution claim is empty. 4.  The negative result framing needs more work . "No universal recipe" is the central claim, but many practitioners already assume this. The paper confirms a suspicion with data but doesn't offer constructive solutions beyond "diagnose your pipeline" — which requires the very G-theory study the paper just demonstrated is expensive (172,800 conditions for one benchmark). Is the recommendation scalable? 5.  Zero figures is unusual and harmful . For a paper about variance decomposition across benchmarks, visual comparisons (stacked bars, heatmaps, radar charts) would dramatically improve readability. The reliance on 11 tables makes the paper harder to parse and less compelling than it could be. 6.  "Fully crossed" is overstated . Only Experiment 1 (MMLU) uses the full crossing (3 precisions × 6 prompts × 6 seeds × 3 temps × 4 orderings). Experiments 2 and the MATH extension use a reduced crossing (2 precisions × 2 temps). This is fine practically but should not be described as a "fully-crossed design spanning 5 benchmarks" in the abstract. 7.  Item dominance on knowledge benchmarks is partially expected from measurement theory . Items in MMLU span from trivially easy to near-impossible across 57 subjects. A large item variance component is expected given this difficulty range. The paper would benefit from contextualizing this against IRT-based item analysis. Questions for Authors : 1.  How does this work relate to Bouthillier et al. (2021), which also decomposed variance in ML benchmarks? 2.  Is the recommendation to run a full G-study per benchmark practical? What is the computational cost, and is there a lightweight diagnostic alternative? 3.  Why were no figures included? The knowledge-reasoning gradient would be far more compelling as a visualization. 4.  Can you release the analysis code alongside the data to substantiate the "diagnostic tool" claim? 5	 timestamp: 2026-05-20 Reviewer R2: Novelty, Related Work, and Significance 1. Summary This paper applies Generalizability Theory (G-theory) to LLM evaluation in a multi-benchmark setting, crossing infrastructure facets (numerical precision, GPU hardware) with methodology facets (prompt template, random seed, temperature, option ordering) and a measurement facet (item selection) across five benchmarks (MMLU, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, GSM8K, MATH), six models (7--14B), and 4M+ evaluation records. Three claims are advanced: (1) a cross-benchmark variance gradient where item_ id share drops monotonically from 56% (MMLU) to 21% (MATH), with CoT stochasticity shifting variance into temperature x item and seed x item interactions; (2) a confirmatory separability null -- direct infrastructure x methodology interactions < 0.3%; (3) D-study protocol reversals showing MMLU is item-limited (420 items for G >= 0.90) while GSM8K is seed-limited (10 seeds), with current practice yielding G  < 0.25 everywhere. Extensions include 14B scale validation, a fine-tuning G-study with RoBERTa-large, and LayerCast precision mitigation. 2. Novelty Assessment Claim 1 (Cross-benchmark variance gradient): Moderate-to-high novelty. This is the paper's strongest novel contribution. No prior work has demonstrated a systematic, monotonic shift in variance structure across multiple benchmarks positioned along a reasoning-intensity continuum. The 35pp gradient from MMLU to MATH, with the mechanistic explanation via CoT stochasticity, is a genuine empirical finding that unifies apparently contradictory conclusions from prior single-benchmark studies (Sclar on prompt sensitivity, Pezeshkpour on ordering, Yuan on precision). The "unifying explanation" framing is well-executed: these studies are not contradictory -- they studied different benchmarks at different positions on the gradient. However, the finding that item_ id dominates is expected from measurement theory (Brennan, 2001, Ch. 3). Any assessment instrument with wide difficulty range will show item variance as the largest source. The paper now acknowledges this appropriately (unlike the earlier draft), but the contribution is in the quantification and the gradient, not in item dominance per se. Claim 2 (Confirmatory separability): Low novelty, moderate utility. This is a confirmatory null result. Infrastructure x methodology interactions are  < 0.3% -- meaning that the infrastructure crossing, which the paper positions as a key methodological advance over Mesting (2026), yields almost nothing. The paper is now honest about this (framing it as "confirmatory" rather than "discovery"), which is the right move. The nuanced decomposition into direct vs. item-conditional interactions (Table 6) adds value: aggregate separability holds, but both factor types interact with items. This is useful methodological validation, but it does not constitute a primary novelty claim. The practical implication is clear: researchers running isolated-factor studies (e.g., studying only prompt sensitivity) can trust their aggregate conclusions, but should be cautious about item-level generalizations. This is valuable guidance even if not surprising. Claim 3 (D-study protocol reversal): Moderate novelty, high practical value. The finding that MMLU needs 420 items while GSM8K needs 10 seeds -- and that the facet effectiveness ratio inverts from 14.2:1 (MMLU) to 0.8:1 (GSM8K) -- is actionable and non-obvious. The "no universal recipe" conclusion directly challenges the standardized evaluation protocols being adopted by leaderboards. The D-study projection grids (Tables 9-10) are the most practically useful output of the paper. The current-practice G  < 0.25 finding is alarming and newsworthy, though its impact depends on whether the community adopts G-theory as a reliability metric. The comparison to educational measurement's G >= 0.80 threshold is effective rhetoric. Collective novelty: The three claims together are stronger than any individual claim. The cross-benchmark gradient (Claim 1) explains the protocol reversal (Claim 3), and the separability null (Claim 2) validates the independent study of each factor type. The narrative coherence is good. The paper is best understood as a large-scale empirical study that applies a well-established framework (G-theory) to a new domain (multi-benchmark LLM evaluation) and discovers a systematic empirical regularity (the gradient). This is a meaningful contribution, though not a methodological breakthrough. Incrementality over Mesting (2026). The paper clearly advances over Mesting in three dimensions: (a) five benchmarks vs. one, (b) infrastructure crossing, (c) model as crossed facet. The infrastructure crossing yields near-null results, so (b) is a confirmatory contribution. The multi-benchmark gradient and model-as-facet analysis are the genuine advances. The paper's four stated differences from Mesting (Section 2, paragraph 3) are accurate and honest. One important difference the paper does not sufficiently emphasize: Mesting found judge identity as the dominant variance source (43.8%), while this paper fixes the judge and finds item_ id dominant. These are complementary findings -- Mesting's design includes judge variance that would dominate everything else; this paper's design excludes judge to reveal the item/methodology/infrastructure structure underneath. This complementarity should be discussed more explicitly. 3. Related Work Completeness The bibliography has improved dramatically from the earlier 7-reference draft to 22 references. The four Related Work paragraphs are well-organized and the positioning against prior work is largely fair and accurate. Adequately covered: -  Variance sources in LLM evaluation (Sclar, Pezeshkpour, Lu, Yuan, Biderman) -- good coverage -  ANOVA-based decomposition (Bouthillier, Henderson, Dodge, Sellam, Dehghani) -- well-positioned -  G-theory in NLP (Mesting, Brennan, Shavelson) -- properly cited with explicit differentiation -  IRT in NLP (Lalor, Rodriguez, Polo, Perlitz) -- good, with IRT/G-theory complementarity noted Missing or under-discussed references: 1.  Nalisnick et al. (2024), GeneralizIT  -- a G-theory software package for ML. Directly relevant to the question of whether this paper's analytical framework is novel or already available as a tool. Should be cited in the G-theory paragraph. 2.  Kunievsky et al. (2025), prompt sensitivity decomposition  -- decomposes prompt variance into intent/articulation/model uncertainty. Relevant to interpreting the prompt x item interaction component. The paper's related_ work_ notes mention it but the paper does not cite it. 3.  Brittlebench (2026)  -- prompt brittleness benchmark, ~ 50% prompt variance. In the project's own literature map but absent from the paper. Directly relevant to the prompt facet findings. 4.  Bui et al. (2025), seed sensitivity in fine-tuning  -- RoBERTa/Llama seed sensitivity study. Directly relevant to Section 8.2 (fine-tuning G-study). In the literature map but not cited. 5.  ThinkingMachines (2025), batch invariance failure  -- 80/1000 unique completions at T=0 from batch-size dependence. The paper uses default vLLM settings without batch-invariant kernels; this reference would explain why seed x item effects are non-zero even at T=0. Not cited. 6.  Vania et al. (2021)  -- IRT item properties in NLP. Listed in the bibliography but not discussed in the Related Work text. Should be integrated into the IRT paragraph. 7.  Mizrahi et al. (2024)  -- cited in the introduction but not in Related Work. Multi-prompt evaluation advocacy. Should appear in the variance sources paragraph. Positioning fairness: The paper's positioning against prior work is generally fair. The claim that "each prior study isolates at most two variance sources" is accurate for the cited studies. The differentiation from Mesting is honest and specific. The IRT/G-theory complementarity framing is appropriate and avoids dismissing IRT work. One concern: the paper states that prior ANOVA-based studies "lack the D-study machinery for projecting reliability under alternative designs." This is technically true but slightly misleading -- bootstrap-based approaches can achieve similar projections without G-theory. The advantage of D-study is its closed-form projections, not that the question is unanswerable otherwise. 4. Significance and Impact Will this paper change how people evaluate LLMs? Partially. The D-study budgets are immediately actionable for benchmark designers and evaluation framework maintainers (e.g., lm-evaluation-harness, HELM). The "G  < 0.25 everywhere" finding is a compelling indictment of current practice. However, adoption depends on: 1.  Whether the community accepts G-theory as the right reliability framework (vs. IRT, bootstrap, or simple confidence intervals) 2.  Whether the computational cost of multi-seed, multi-prompt evaluation is acceptable 3.  Whether leaderboard operators are incentivized to change practices The paper would benefit from a concrete comparison: "Running MMLU with the recommended budget (420 items, 3 prompts, 2 seeds = 2,520 evaluations) costs X GPU-hours per model, compared to Y GPU-hours for current practice." Without cost estimates, the budgets are theoretical. Are the D-study budgets practically useful? Yes, with caveats. The specific numbers (420 items for MMLU, 10 seeds for GSM8K) are directly useful. The facet effectiveness ratios (Table 12) provide a decision framework. The projection grids (Tables 9-10) allow practitioners to find their own cost-reliability tradeoff. The main limitation is that the budgets are derived from 7-14B open-weight models. API-based models (GPT-4, Claude) may have different variance structures due to opaque infrastructure, quantization, and routing. The paper acknowledges this but does not quantify the risk. Is "no universal recipe" surprising or obvious? Moderately surprising in its specificity. The qualitative intuition that "different benchmarks might need different protocols" is not new. But the quantitative demonstration that the facet effectiveness ratio inverts from 14.2:1 to 0.8:1 across benchmarks, and that the same practitioner should use 420 items + 2 seeds for MMLU but 150 items + 10 seeds for GSM8K, is non-obvious and actionable. The counter-intuitive finding that knowledge benchmarks yield lower G than reasoning benchmarks (MMLU 0.36 vs. GSM8K 0.55 under full factorial) is genuinely surprising and well-explained. 5. Framing and Narrative Strengths: -  The three-claim structure is clean and well-supported. -  The "unifying explanation" framing for the gradient is effective. -  The Discussion section is balanced, with a thorough Limitations paragraph. -  The engine confound discovery is presented with appropriate before/after validation. -  The paper correctly frames infrastructure crossing as confirmatory rather than primary novelty. Weaknesses: -  Zero figures.  This is a serious deficiency for a variance decomposition paper. The distilled writing patterns from this field identify stacked-bar charts as an expected idiom (Mesting, Brittlebench). The cross-benchmark gradient (Table 5) would be far more compelling as a stacked-bar figure. The D-study projections (Tables 9-10) cry out for line plots of G vs. facet allocation. The facet effectiveness inversion (Table 12) would be intuitive as a crossing-lines plot. With 14 tables and 0 figures, the paper is dense and visually monotonous. This is a competitive disadvantage at a top venue. -  The paper title promises "Evaluation Metrics" but delivers only binary scoring.  The abstract and main text focus entirely on binary correct scoring. Logprob-based scoring is relegated to a one-paragraph appendix (Appendix B). The paper framing documents mention "metric-conditional budgets" as a core claim, but the submitted paper has largely abandoned this dimension. Either deliver the metric analysis or remove "Evaluation Metrics" from the title. -  The fine-tuning section (8.2) feels bolted on.  RoBERTa-large fine-tuning on SST-2/MNLI/RTE/COPA is architecturally distant from the 7-14B decoder inference setting. The variance hierarchy comparison (Table 15) is interesting but the cross-paradigm generalization is weak. This section would be stronger as a standalone follow-up study or should be explicitly qualified as "preliminary evidence." 6. Scope Concerns Is 5 benchmarks x 6 models x 7-14B sufficient? For the cross-benchmark gradient: yes, 5 benchmarks spanning knowledge-to-reasoning is adequate. The monotonic gradient with non-overlapping bootstrap CIs (Table 8) provides statistical support. Adding more benchmarks (e.g., GPQA, TruthfulQA, HumanEval) would strengthen the gradient but is not strictly necessary. For model generality: the 4 x 7-9B models show consistent patterns (per-model tables confirm the gradient within each model), and the 14B extension (Section 8.1) falls within the 8B range. However: 1.  No 70B+ models.  Larger models may have qualitatively different variance structures (e.g., higher accuracy compresses item_ id, stronger reasoning reduces CoT stochasticity). The paper cannot claim generality beyond the 7-14B scale. 2.  No proprietary API models.  GPT-4, Claude, Gemini have opaque infrastructure (unknown precision, routing, batching). The separability null may not hold when infrastructure is uncontrolled. Mesting (2026) studied API models; this paper studies open-weight models. The complementarity is noted but not deeply explored. 3.  No non-English benchmarks.  All five benchmarks are English-only. Cross-lingual variance structure could differ systematically (e.g., tokenization effects on item difficulty). 4.  No generation-based benchmarks.  All benchmarks are multiple-choice or short-answer. Open-ended generation tasks (summarization, translation, creative writing) may have fundamentally different variance structures where temperature and seed effects dominate even more. 5.  Only 200 items per benchmark.  MMLU has ~ 14K items, GSM8K has ~ 8K. The 200-item stratified sample captures the difficulty distribution but may miss tail effects. The resampling stability test (Section 4.3) partially addresses this but only for MMLU. 7. Strengths (bulleted) -  Cross-benchmark variance gradient is a genuine, well-supported empirical contribution  that unifies contradictory findings from prior single-benchmark studies. The monotonic 35pp gradient from MMLU to MATH, with mechanistic explanation via CoT stochasticity, is the paper's signature finding. -  Massive experimental scale : 4M+ evaluation records, 5 benchmarks, 6 models, crossed factorial designs. Few empirical papers in this area match the breadth. -  D-study reproducibility budgets are immediately actionable : specific item/prompt/seed allocations for G >= 0.90, benchmark-specific, with projection grids for cost-reliability tradeoffs. -  Engine confound discovery and correction  (vLLM V0 vs. V1 routing for different precisions) is a standalone methodological contribution valuable to any researcher comparing precision modes. -  Honest framing of the separability null : infrastructure crossing framed as confirmatory rather than primary novelty, with nuanced decomposition into aggregate vs. item-conditional interactions. -  Comprehensive robustness checks : item resampling stability, REML vs. Henderson III comparison, bootstrap CIs, per-model breakdowns, 14B scale validation, cross-estimation-method concordance. -  Bibliography substantially improved  over earlier drafts: 22 references covering variance sources, ANOVA decomposition, G-theory, and IRT literature. -  Counter-intuitive G pattern  (knowledge benchmarks yield lower G than reasoning benchmarks) is well-explained and adds insight beyond the headline gradient finding. 8. Weaknesses (bulleted) -  Zero figures in a variance decomposition paper  is a serious presentation deficiency. Stacked-bar charts, D-study curves, and gradient visualizations are expected field idioms (Mesting 2026, Brittlebench 2026). 14 tables + 0 figures makes the paper dense and hard to scan. -  Infrastructure crossing is the claimed methodological advance over Mesting but yields near-null results  ( < 0.3% direct interactions). The main findings (gradient, D-study budgets) would emerge from a Mesting-style design with fixed infrastructure. The paper is honest about this but it weakens the novelty argument. -  Title promises "Evaluation Metrics" but the paper delivers only binary scoring  in the main text. Logprob analysis is a one-paragraph appendix. The metric-conditional dimension from the paper framing is largely absent. -  No models above 14B.  Larger models may compress item_ id and reduce CoT stochasticity, potentially altering the gradient. Generality claims should be scoped to 7-14B. -  Fine-tuning extension (RoBERTa-large, encoder-only, classification)  is architecturally distant from the decoder inference setting. Cross-paradigm generalization is weak; the section feels appended rather than integrated. -  Missing references : GeneralizIT (2024), Kunievsky et al. (2025), Brittlebench (2026), Bui et al. (2025), ThinkingMachines (2025) -- all in the project's own literature map but absent from the paper. These are relevant to the G-theory tooling, prompt decomposition, and fine-tuning variance discussions. -  No cost analysis for recommended budgets.  The D-study projections recommend specific item/prompt/seed allocations but do not estimate the GPU-hour cost of implementing these recommendations. Without cost, the budgets are theoretical. -  200-item samples from much larger benchmarks.  Resampling stability is tested only for MMLU. The other four benchmarks lack resampling validation, leaving open the possibility that the gradient is partially driven by item sampling artifacts on specific benchmarks. 9. Questions for Authors 1.  The cross-benchmark gradient is your strongest finding. Could you demonstrate that it holds under logprob-based scoring as well? The one-paragraph Appendix B suggests item_ id drops to 42.8% on MMLU, but does the full gradient (MMLU > ARC > HellaSwag > GSM8K > MATH) hold under logprob scoring? If not, is the gradient an artifact of binary scoring thresholds? 2.  Your D-study recommends 420 items + 3 prompts + 2 seeds for MMLU (2,520 total evaluations). How does this compare to Polo et al.'s tinyBenchmarks recommendation for MMLU? If IRT-based subsampling achieves reliable rankings with fewer items, what does G-theory add? 3.  DeepSeek-R1-Distill-14B shows elevated temperature x item (8.8%) and seed x item (5.2%) on MMLU -- above the 8B range (Table 13). You attribute this to "reasoning distillation introducing implicit chain-of-thought tendencies." Can you verify this mechanistically? Does DeepSeek-R1-Distill-14B produce longer or more variable outputs on MMLU items compared to the other models? 4.  The separability null holds for 2 GPU types (Section 6). How confident are you that this extends to, say, A100 vs. H100 vs. B200 comparisons where the architectural differences (TF32 tensor cores, FP8 support, different memory bandwidth) are more substantial than between two GPUs of similar generation? 5.  You fix the judge model, unlike Mesting who includes judge as a facet. Since Mesting found judge identity as the dominant source (43.8%), your entire variance structure sits "underneath" the judge variance. How should practitioners interpret your budgets if they use LLM-as-judge evaluation (increasingly common)? Would your gradient hold if judge were included as a facet, or would judge variance dominate and flatten the cross-benchmark differences? 6.  The fine-tuning G-study finds item_ id at rank-1 across all tasks (35.8-43.8%). But Bui et al. (2025) report extreme seed variance (RTES variance = 18.22) for RoBERTa on RTE. How do your RTE fine-tuning results compare to Bui et al.? Are the magnitudes consistent? 7.  Current-practice G  < 0.25 is your most alarming finding. Have you computed what fraction of published leaderboard rankings would change if evaluations were repeated with different seeds/prompts? A "rank instability" analysis (e.g., what percentage of model-pair orderings flip under re-evaluation) would make the inadequacy finding more concrete than an abstract G coefficient. 8.  The paper uses Henderson's Method III with REML as sensitivity check and reports they agree within 1.4pp. Have you considered Bayesian variance component estimation (e.g., via Stan or brms)? This would give full posterior distributions on variance components rather than point estimates + bootstrap CIs, and would handle the near-zero infrastructure components more gracefully. 10. Minor Issues -  Table 5 header says "4 models pooled" but the design description mentions "4 models x 2 precisions x ..." -- clarify whether model is pooled or crossed in this analysis. -  Table 7 (5-benchmark gradient) shows G_ full for GSM8K (0.55) higher than MATH (0.50), breaking the monotonic pattern. The text does not explain this reversal; add a brief note. -  The abstract says "over 4 million evaluation records" but summing the reported record counts (1,036,800 + 1,382,400 + 460,800 + 691,200 + 345,600 + 172,800 + fine-tuning) exceeds 4M. Provide an exact total or say "approximately." -  Section 3.2 says "2-3 levels" for temperature but does not specify which benchmarks use 2 vs. 3 levels. Clarify. -  Table 1 (MMLU variance): the "infra x method" row aggregates multiple interaction terms. Break this out or provide the individual terms in an appendix. -  The paper references "Section 7" (comprehensive analysis) as Section \ref{sec:comprehensive} but the numbering in the LaTeX may not match if figures are added later. Verify cross-references. -  Appendix C on higher-order interactions is interesting (temp x seed x item = 1.8%) but could be expanded. Does this three-way interaction show a benchmark gradient similar to the two-way interactions? 11. Counter-intuitive G pattern  (knowledge benchmarks yield lower G than reasoning benchmarks) is well-explained and insightful. 9.  Current-practice G<0.25  is an important and alarming finding for the field. 9. Consolidated Weaknesses Major 1.  Binary data in standard G-theory  without discussion of the methodological limitation. Item_ id dominance is partially artifactual from the Bernoulli variance function. Must be addressed in revision. 2.  Zero figures in a variance decomposition paper.  19 tables and 0 figures. Stacked-bar charts, D-study curves, and gradient visualizations are expected idioms. Serious competitive disadvantage at a top venue. 3.  Temperature (2–3 levels) and ordering (4 systematic rotations) as random facets  is statistically dubious. Sensitivity analysis with these as fixed effects is needed. Moderate 4.  Asymmetric designs across benchmarks  confound cross-benchmark precision comparisons (FP32 absent from non-MMLU experiments). 5.  Separability claim overstated in abstract  — holds on knowledge benchmarks but GSM8K (3.0%) and MATH (2.5%) exceed the stated threshold. Should be qualified. 6.  Title promises "Evaluation Metrics" but delivers only binary scoring  in main text. Logprob analysis relegated to one-paragraph appendix. 7.  Infrastructure crossing is the claimed advance over Mesting but yields near-null results.  The main findings would emerge from a Mesting-style design with fixed infrastructure. 8.  No models above 14B.  Generality cannot be claimed beyond this scale range. 9.  Missing references:  GeneralizIT, Kunievsky et al. (2025), Brittlebench (2026), Bui et al. (2025), ThinkingMachines (2025). 10.  Fine-tuning extension (RoBERTa-large, encoder-only)  is architecturally distant from decoder inference. Feels appended rather than integrated. Minor 11.  No cost analysis for recommended D-study budgets. 12.  Residual component (6–18%) is underanalyzed; higher-order interactions mentioned but not tabulated. 13.  14B extension is underpowered (2 models, 1 df for model effects). 14.  Item resampling stability tested only for MMLU, not for other benchmarks. 15.  Prompt template text not provided; reproducibility details (vLLM commit hash, model weight hashes, CUDA versions) insufficient. 10. Consolidated Questions for Authors 1.  Binary data:  How do you address the assumption violation of applying Henderson III / REML to binary (0/1) responses? Have you considered generalized G-theory or a probit/logit link-function decomposition? Does item_ id dominance survive under a method appropriate for binary data? 2.  Temperature as random facet:  What justifies treating 2–3 temperature levels (specific design points: 0, 0.5, 1.0) as a random rather than fixed facet? Have you compared results with temperature as fixed? 3.  Cross-benchmark precision confound:  Have you re-analyzed MMLU restricted to BF16/FP16 only (excluding FP32) for the cross-benchmark comparison? Does the precision gradient survive with matched precision levels? 4.  Gradient under logprob scoring:  Does the full 5-benchmark gradient (MMLU > ARC > HellaSwag > GSM8K > MATH) hold under logprob-based scoring? If not, is the gradient partially an artifact of binary scoring thresholds? 5.  Comparison with IRT:  How do the D-study budgets compare to Polo et al.'s tinyBenchmarks recommendations for MMLU? What does G-theory add over IRT-based efficient subsampling? 6.  Separability scope:  How confident are you that the separability null extends to more diverse hardware (A100 vs. H100 vs. B200) where architectural differences are more substantial? 7.  Judge variance complementarity:  Your entire variance structure sits "underneath" Mesting's judge variance (43.8%). How should practitioners interpret your budgets for LLM-as-judge evaluation? Would the gradient hold if judge were included as a facet? 8.  Negative variance estimates:  How are negative Henderson III estimates handled (set to zero, left negative, redistributed)? This affects the separability claim where infra×method components are near zero. 9.  D-study optimization procedure:  How were the "optimal" prompt and seed counts determined? Formal cost minimization, or chosen by inspection? 10.  Rank instability analysis:  Have you computed what fraction of published leaderboard rankings would change under re-evaluation with different seeds/prompts? This would make G <0.25 more concrete than an abstract coefficient. 11. Recommended Revisions (Priority-Ordered) Must-fix for acceptance 1.  Add 3–5 figures: (a) cross-benchmark stacked-bar gradient, (b) D-study G vs. total evaluations curves, (c) facet effectiveness ratio visualization, (d) bootstrap CI forest plot. 2.  Add a paragraph discussing binary data limitations in G-theory estimation and note that logprob scoring provides the methodologically cleaner decomposition. 3.  Present sensitivity analysis with temperature as fixed facet. 4.  Qualify separability claim in abstract: " <0.3% on knowledge benchmarks; rises to 2–3% on reasoning benchmarks." Should-fix 5.  Re-analyze MMLU at BF16/FP16 only for the cross-benchmark comparison table. 6.  Add the 5 missing references (GeneralizIT, Kunievsky, Brittlebench, Bui, ThinkingMachines). 7.  Align title with content: either deliver metric-conditional analysis or remove "Evaluation Metrics" from title. 8.  Add prompt template text in an appendix; provide vLLM commit hash, model weight hashes. Nice-to-have 9.  Extend logprob analysis to all 5 benchmarks to test whether the gradient holds under continuous scoring. 10.  Add cost estimates (GPU-hours) for recommended D-study budgets. 11.  Expand higher-order interaction analysis in appendix. 12. Overall Assessment Score: 4/6 (Weak Accept) Confidence: High Meta-Review Justification Both reviewers independently scored this paper 4/6 (Weak Accept) with high confidence, and the roundtable did not identify grounds to change this. The cross-benchmark variance gradient is a genuine novel finding: no prior work has demonstrated the systematic shift from item-dominated (knowledge tasks) to interaction-dominated (reasoning tasks) variance structure, and the 35pp gradient with non-overlapping bootstrap CIs is well-supported. The D-study reproducibility budgets fill a real practical gap, and the G <0.25 indictment of current practice is alarming and important. The paper is held back by addressable issues: (a) zero figures is a serious presentation weakness at a top venue; (b) binary data in standard G-theory requires explicit discussion; (c) temperature/ordering as random facets needs sensitivity analysis; and (d) the separability claim needs scoping. None of these are fatal. If the must-fix revisions are made — especially adding figures and the binary data discussion — the paper would likely move to 5/6 (Accept). The infrastructure crossing, positioned as the key methodological advance over Mesting, yields near-null results. This is intellectually honest (confirmatory null) but means the paper's primary novelty rests on the cross-benchmark gradient and D-study budgets rather than on the infrastructure-methodology crossing. Both reviewers agree this is sufficient for a top venue, given the scale of the empirical contribution and the practical utility of the findings. Bottom line:  A well-executed, large-scale empirical study with a genuine novel finding (the gradient), actionable outputs (D-study budgets), and an important policy implication (G <0.25). At the acceptance threshold; fixable revisions would push it to a clear accept.

4	 timestamp: 2026-05-20T23:45:00+00:00 Dream Review Report — R1 (Methodology & Experimental Rigor) Paper:  Reproducibility Budgets for LLM Evaluation: A Generalizability Theory Analysis of Variance Sources Across Benchmarks, Models, and Evaluation Metrics Tier:  Median Review mode:  R1 focus — Methodology, Experimental Design, Statistical Rigor 1. Paper Summary The paper applies Generalizability Theory (G-theory) to LLM evaluation, conducting multi-benchmark crossed-facet variance decompositions across five benchmarks (MMLU, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, GSM8K, MATH), six models (4x7-9B + 2x14B), two GPU architectures, and multiple levels of precision, prompt template, seed, temperature, and answer ordering. Over 3 million evaluation records are analyzed. Three claims are made: (1) a benchmark-conditional variance gradient where item dominance ranges from 48% (MMLU) to 28% (MATH) under model-as-facet analysis; (2) infrastructure x methodology separability at the aggregate level ( <0.5% on knowledge benchmarks, rising to 3% on math-generation benchmarks); (3) metric-conditional, benchmark-specific reproducibility budgets via D-study projections. Extensions cover 14B models, RoBERTa fine-tuning, LayerCast precision mitigation, and three scoring metrics. 2. Methodological Soundness 2.1 G-Theory Framework Application Largely correct, with one significant improvement over Dream #1.  The revised paper treats model as a crossed random facet (Section 4.4 / Table 5), which was the most critical methodological concern in the prior review. This properly separates model×item interaction (16-22%) from pure item variance and residual. The 4pp systematic reduction across all benchmarks is plausible and consistent with psychometric expectation when objects of measurement have heterogeneous difficulty profiles. Henderson Method III vs. REML.  The paper uses Henderson Method III (expected mean squares) as primary estimation with REML as sensitivity check. This is defensible: Henderson III is unbiased for balanced designs, and the design is nearly balanced (fully crossed within each experiment). The reported max divergence of 2.1pp with preserved rank ordering is reassuring. However: -  Concern:  Henderson Method III can produce negative variance component estimates for near-zero components. The MATH table (Table 22 in the imagined experiments) shows a negative "other" entry (-1.5%), which is characteristic of this issue. The paper should explicitly state how negative estimates are handled (set to zero? redistributed? left as-is?). This matters for the separability claim where infra×method components are near zero — a negative estimate truncated to zero looks different from a genuinely zero estimate. -  Concern:  The G-theory formula presented in Equation 2 is simplified. The actual D-study formula for a multi-facet crossed design with 5+ facets involves many more terms. The paper should either present the full formula used or cite a specific implementation (e.g., GeneralizIT package). The simplified formula risks misleading readers about how D-study projections were actually computed. 2.2 Crossed Random-Effects Assumptions Items as random facet:  Justified. The 200 items per benchmark are sampled (stratified) from larger pools (MMLU: 14,042; ARC: 2,590; GSM8K: 1,319; HellaSwag: 10,042; MATH: 5,000). The random-facet assumption requires that observed items are exchangeable draws from a universe of admissible observations. Stratified sampling strengthens this by ensuring subject/topic coverage. Model as random facet:  Partially justified. Four 7-9B models from different families (Qwen, Llama, Gemma, Mistral) are treated as exchangeable draws from the universe of "7-9B instruction-tuned LLMs." This is defensible but arguable — the model universe is not well-defined, and four models provide limited degrees of freedom for estimating model-related variance components. The 14B extension (2 models) is even more constrained. The paper should acknowledge that model-as-facet with k=4 yields imprecise estimates of model variance components and that the model universe is narrowly defined (open-weight, instruction-tuned, 7-9B). Prompt as random facet:  The 6 prompt templates are described but their generation process matters for the random-effects assumption. If they were systematically designed to vary specific dimensions (e.g., formality, instruction explicitness), they may not represent random draws from a prompt universe. The paper should clarify whether prompt templates were generated to be representative (supporting random effects) or to maximize diversity (which biases variance estimates upward). Seed as random facet:  Clearly justified — seeds are arbitrary integers drawn from a large space. Temperature as random facet:  Problematic. With only 2-3 levels (e.g., 0, 0.5, 1.0), treating temperature as a random facet is statistically dubious — these are specific points chosen to span the parameter range, not random draws from a temperature distribution. Temperature is better modeled as fixed. If treated as random, the variance estimates carry extreme uncertainty with 2-3 df. The paper should address this. Ordering as random facet:  Four orderings (ABCD, BCDA, CDAB, DABC) — these are systematic rotations, not random draws. The random-effects assumption is defensible only if one argues these represent exchangeable draws from the universe of possible orderings, which is reasonable for 4-option MC but should be noted. 2.3 Variance Estimation for Binary Data Critical methodological question.  Binary correct (0/1) data violates the normality assumption underlying standard G-theory variance component estimation. Henderson Method III and REML both assume continuous, approximately normal response variables. For binary data: -  Variance components are bounded by the Bernoulli variance p(1-p), creating ceiling effects for items near p=0 or p=1. -  Item-level variance is mechanically linked to item difficulty — easy and hard items contribute less variance by construction, inflating the apparent dominance of "mid-difficulty" items. -  The paper's finding that item_ id is the largest variance source is partially an artifact of using binary scoring on items with heterogeneous difficulty. This is the well-known "item difficulty confound" in classical test theory. The text-exact-match metric (also binary) and logprob metric (continuous) provide useful sensitivity checks. The logprob result (item_ id = 55%) is methodologically cleaner because the response variable is continuous, avoiding the binary data issue. The paper should discuss the binary data limitation explicitly and note that logprob scoring provides the most methodologically sound variance decomposition. 3. Experimental Design 3.1 Factorial Design Adequacy MMLU (Exp 1): Strong.  4 models × 3 precisions × 6 prompts × 6 seeds × 3 temperatures × 4 orderings × 200 items = 1,036,800 observations. This is the richest design and supports all claimed decompositions. The V0 enforce_ eager control eliminates the engine confound — this is excellent experimental hygiene. Cross-benchmark (Exp 3): Adequate but reduced.  2 precisions × 2 temperatures (vs. 3×3 on MMLU). The reduction is justified by compute constraints but creates an asymmetry: FP32 is absent from cross-benchmark experiments, meaning the precision facet is restricted to BF16/FP16 (which differ minimally). The claimed cross-benchmark gradient in precision effects (MMLU 3.0% vs. GSM8K 1.0%) is confounded with the different precision levels tested. This should be explicitly acknowledged. Multi-hardware (Exp 4): Adequate.  2 GPU types is the minimum for estimating hardware effects. With 1 df for hardware main effect, the estimate is necessarily imprecise. The paper correctly frames hardware findings as directional rather than definitive. Item resampling (Exp 2): Well-designed.  Three independent stratified draws with different seeds. The CV=0.19 (paper) or CV=0.19 (imagined experiments) on item_ id is an important honesty result. However, three draws provide only a rough estimate of resampling variability — 10+ draws would be more convincing, though the compute cost may be prohibitive. Fine-tuning (Exp 7): Adequate for its scope.  432 runs per task × 4 tasks = 1,728 total. The fully crossed design (seed × LR × shuffle × GPU × precision) is clean. The RoBERTa-large choice is acknowledged as a limitation (encoder-only, classification). This experiment is best framed as a conceptual extension rather than a direct generalization. 3.2 Missing Controls and Confounds 1.  Batch size / sequence length confound.  vLLM batches requests dynamically. If different benchmark items produce different output lengths (especially GSM8K/MATH with CoT), batch composition may vary, introducing an unmodeled variance source that gets absorbed into residual or item interactions. The paper uses "default vLLM settings" which is realistic but means batch-level nondeterminism is present. 2.  Prompt template × benchmark interaction.  The same 6 prompt templates are used across benchmarks, but their appropriateness may vary by task. A prompt template that works well for MMLU factual recall may be poorly suited for GSM8K math reasoning. This could inflate prompt×item interactions on some benchmarks for reasons unrelated to the "prompt sensitivity" construct. 3.  Item difficulty distribution differs across benchmarks.  MMLU items span a wide difficulty range; GSM8K items at 8B model scale cluster near 0.4-0.6 accuracy; MATH items are heavily bimodal (trivial or impossible for 8B models). These distributional differences mechanically affect how much variance is attributable to items vs. interactions. The paper's "cognitive complexity" explanation for the cross-benchmark gradient is plausible but not the only explanation — difficulty distribution differences could account for part of the pattern. 4.  Stratified sampling details.  The paper mentions stratified sampling across 57 MMLU subjects, but the stratification scheme for other benchmarks (GSM8K difficulty levels? MATH topics?) is not described. If non-MMLU benchmarks lack stratification, their item samples may be less representative. 5.  Answer extraction method.  For generation-based scoring, the method of extracting answers from generated text is a potential confound. Different regex/parsing strategies could produce different binary scores for the same generation. This is not discussed. 3.3 Item Sampling Strategy The 200-item stratified sample from MMLU's 14,042 items (1.4%) is a reasonable balance between compute cost and representativeness. The resampling stability test (CV=0.19) properly quantifies the sampling uncertainty. For other benchmarks: -  GSM8K: 200/1,319 = 15.2% — much denser sampling, less sampling uncertainty expected. -  ARC-Challenge: 200/2,590 = 7.7% — moderate. -  HellaSwag: 200/10,042 = 2.0% — similar to MMLU. -  MATH: 200/5,000 = 4.0% — moderate. The paper should note that cross-benchmark comparisons of item_ id variance share are confounded with sampling fraction — benchmarks with denser item sampling (GSM8K) mechanically have lower item-sampling uncertainty, which could affect the D-study projections. 4. Statistical Rigor 4.1 Bootstrap Confidence Intervals Construction:  1,000 item×condition resamples. This is a standard nonparametric bootstrap for G-theory (cf. Brennan, 2001, Ch. 10). The resampling unit matters: resampling items treats items as the primary sampling unit, which is appropriate given that item selection is the largest variance source. Concerns: -  The bootstrap resamples items but holds conditions (prompt, seed, temp, precision, ordering) fixed. This captures item-sampling uncertainty but not condition-sampling uncertainty. A more thorough approach would resample both items and conditions (double bootstrap), though this is computationally expensive and rarely done in G-theory applications. The paper should acknowledge this limitation. -  The reported CI widths (~ 0.14 for item_ id) are wide enough that the practical implications change substantially across the CI range. For example, MMLU item_ id [ 0.41, 0.55] maps to different D-study recommendations at each endpoint. The paper handles this well by reporting D-study CIs ([ 350, 510 ] for G≥0.90 on MMLU). 4.2 D-Study Projections Validity:  D-study projections assume that variance components estimated from the G-study generalize to the projected design. This is the standard G-theory assumption and is reasonable when the projected design changes only the number of levels (e.g., more items, more seeds) rather than the nature of the facets. The projections in Table 8 change item counts while holding prompt/seed counts at "optimal" levels — this is valid. Concern — optimal prompt/seed counts.  The D-study recommends "3 prompts / 4 seeds" for MMLU and "4 prompts / 6 seeds" for GSM8K. How are these "optimal" counts determined? If they are chosen to minimize total compute for a target G, the optimization procedure should be described. If they are chosen post-hoc to make the item counts look reasonable, this is problematic. Concern — extrapolation to 420+ items.  The G-study uses 200 items. Projecting to 420 items assumes linear scaling of the error reduction, which holds under the random-sampling model. However, if the additional 220 items are drawn from the same pool, they may not be independent of the original 200 (especially for smaller pools like GSM8K with only 1,319 total items). The finite-population correction should be applied when the projected sample is a large fraction of the universe. 4.3 REML Sensitivity Check Sufficient for its purpose.  The 2.1pp maximum divergence with preserved rankings is adequate evidence that the choice between Henderson III and REML does not affect qualitative conclusions. However, REML is generally preferred for unbalanced designs. Since the within-experiment designs are balanced (fully crossed), Henderson III is appropriate. The sensitivity check confirms this. 4.4 Permutation Test for Gradient The p=0.003 for the gradient direction (MMLU > HellaSwag on item_ id) is properly reported. The paper correctly notes that the CIs overlap partially at the margins ([ 0.38, 0.41 ]), supporting directional but not magnitude claims. This is honest and appropriate. 5. Reproducibility Concerns 1.  vLLM version dependency.  The paper uses vLLM 0.9.2 with V0 enforce_ eager. vLLM's behavior changes across versions (the V0/V1 engine confound demonstrates this). The results may not replicate on vLLM 0.8.x or 1.0.x. The paper should pin the exact vLLM commit hash, not just the version number. 2.  Model weight provenance.  The paper lists model names but not specific weight versions (e.g., HuggingFace revision hashes). Model weights on HuggingFace can be updated without changing the model card name. For reproducibility, exact weight hashes are needed. 3.  CUDA version and driver.  CUDA nondeterminism is a core topic of the paper. The exact CUDA version, cuDNN version, and driver version should be reported. The paper mentions "CUDA 12.8" support for vLLM 0.9.2 but does not pin the exact software stack. 4.  Item sample seeds.  The stratified sampling seeds for the 200-item samples should be released. The resampling stability test uses seeds 0, 7, 99 — are these the only seeds tested? If the main experiments use a single seed (e.g., seed 0), the results are conditional on that particular draw. 5.  Prompt template text.  The 6 prompt templates are critical to reproducibility but their exact text is not provided in the paper. They should appear in an appendix. 6. Strengths -  Comprehensive factorial design.  The MMLU experiment (1,036,800 observations, 5,184 conditions) is one of the largest crossed factorial designs in LLM evaluation research. The systematic approach — full crossing on MMLU, reduced crossing on other benchmarks, explicit confound controls — reflects careful experimental planning. -  Engine confound discovery and fix.  Identifying that default vLLM routes FP32 through a different engine (V1 CUDA graph) than BF16/FP16 (V0 eager) is a standalone methodological contribution. The enforce_ eager fix is simple, actionable, and immediately useful to the community. -  Model-as-facet analysis.  This revision correctly treats model as a crossed random facet, addressing the most fundamental concern from Dream #1. The systematic 4pp reduction across all benchmarks and the extraction of 16-22% model×item interaction is a clean result. -  Multi-benchmark coverage.  Five benchmarks spanning knowledge retrieval (MMLU, ARC), commonsense reasoning (HellaSwag), arithmetic reasoning (GSM8K), and proof reasoning (MATH) provides genuine coverage of the LLM evaluation landscape. The three-tier clustering is more nuanced than a simple monotonic gradient. -  Metric-conditional analysis.  The binary/text-match/logprob comparison (Table 9) is a first-order finding: G ranges from 0.32 to 0.97 depending on the scoring metric. This alone justifies the paper — practitioners cannot discuss "reliability" without specifying the metric. -  Honest uncertainty quantification.  Bootstrap CIs on variance components, D-study CIs on item counts, resampling stability tests, and REML sensitivity checks collectively demonstrate statistical maturity. The paper acknowledges that the gradient is directional rather than precisely quantified. -  Three-tier narrative is stronger than two-cluster.  Including MATH extends the gradient from {MMLU, ARC} vs. {GSM8K, HellaSwag} to a three-tier structure with 20pp spread, providing more evidence for the benchmark-conditional story. -  Separability as confirmatory null.  Reframing infrastructure×methodology separability as a confirmatory result (validating prior isolated-factor studies) rather than a breakthrough is intellectually honest and strengthens the paper's credibility. -  Fine-tuning contrast.  The inverted variance hierarchy (LR/seed dominate in fine-tuning vs. items dominate in inference) adds conceptual depth and explains why different evaluation modes have different reproducibility conventions. 7. Weaknesses Major -  Binary data in G-theory.  Applying standard G-theory variance component estimation (Henderson III / REML) to binary (0/1) data is methodologically questionable. The response variable violates normality and homoscedasticity assumptions. Item variance is mechanically linked to item difficulty via the Bernoulli variance function. This affects the headline item_ id estimates and all downstream D-study projections. The logprob analysis partially mitigates this, but the paper's primary analysis is on binary data. A generalized G-theory approach (Brennan, 2001, Ch. 12) or a link-function-based decomposition would be more appropriate. At minimum, the paper must discuss this limitation and note that item dominance under binary scoring is partially artifactual. -  Temperature and ordering as random facets.  With 2-3 temperature levels and 4 systematic ordering rotations, treating these as random facets is questionable. Random-effects estimation requires the observed levels to be exchangeable draws from a larger universe. Temperature levels (0, 0.5, 1.0) are specific design points, not random draws from a temperature distribution. The 4 orderings are systematic rotations, not random permutations of 4 !=24 possibilities. Misspecifying fixed effects as random inflates the estimated variance components for these facets and their interactions. The paper should either (a) justify the random-effects assumption for these facets, (b) treat them as fixed and re-estimate, or (c) present both analyses as a sensitivity check. -  Asymmetric designs across benchmarks weaken cross-benchmark claims.  MMLU uses 3 precisions × 3 temperatures; other benchmarks use 2 × 2. FP32 is absent from non-MMLU experiments. This means precision-related variance on MMLU includes the FP32 degradation effect that is absent from other benchmarks. The claimed gradient in precision effects (MMLU 3.0% → MATH 0.5%) is confounded with the different precision levels tested. The paper should either (a) re-analyze MMLU restricted to BF16/FP16 for the cross-benchmark comparison, or (b) explicitly state the confound. -  Separability claim is benchmark-conditional but presented as a general finding.  The abstract and contributions list separability as " <0.5% binary" but the body reveals GSM8K reaches 3.0% and MATH reaches 2.5%. A finding that holds on 3/5 benchmarks but fails on 2/5 is not a general separability result — it is a benchmark-conditional one. The abstract and conclusions should lead with the conditionality. Moderate -  D-study "optimal" prompt/seed counts are not derived.  The paper presents specific prompt and seed counts (3/4 for MMLU, 4/6 for GSM8K) as "optimal" without showing the optimization procedure. Are these the minimum counts that don't substantially change the D-study item projection? Are they from a cost-minimization formula? The derivation matters because practitioners will use these numbers directly. -  Residual component is large and underanalyzed.  Residual ranges from 6% to 18% across benchmarks and analyses. Under model-as-facet analysis, the residual on MMLU drops from 14% to 8%, which is progress, but 8% is still substantial. What is in this residual? Higher-order interactions (3-way and above) are mentioned in passing ("3-5% total") but not tabulated. The paper claims higher-order interactions are small, but 3-5% is comparable to many named 2-way interactions (e.g., seed×item at 2.0%). An appendix breaking down the residual would strengthen the paper. -  HellaSwag clustering with GSM8K is not well-explained.  HellaSwag is a commonsense reasoning / sentence completion task, not a math reasoning task. Its item_ id (31%) places it in the same tier as GSM8K (36%), but its infra×method (0.3%) is similar to knowledge benchmarks. The paper groups them in a "mid" tier based on item_ id alone, but the infra×method pattern suggests HellaSwag behaves differently from GSM8K. The three-tier narrative is cleaner than the data fully support. -  14B extension is underpowered.  With only 2 models, model-as-facet analysis has essentially 1 df for model effects. The reported model×item = 25% (vs. 21% at 8B) could reflect the specific model pair chosen (dense vs. reasoning-distilled) rather than a scale effect. The paper should note that the 8B→14B comparison confounds scale with architecture diversity. -  No correction for multiple comparisons.  Many variance components are tested across many benchmarks and metrics. While the bootstrap CIs provide individual component uncertainty, no family-wise error correction is applied. The GSM8K infra×method CI [ 0.012, 0.048 ] excludes zero, but is this still significant after correcting for testing the same hypothesis on 5 benchmarks? Minor -  "Over 3 million" vs. "over 4 million."  The abstract says "over 3 million"; the best-tier paper says "over 4 million." The actual count should be computed and reported exactly. -  MATH "other" = -1.5%.  Negative variance component estimates should be flagged and the handling policy stated (see Section 2.1 above). -  LayerCast section (8.3) adds little.  The finding that LayerCast provides marginal benefit over BF16 is expected given that precision effects are already small. This could be condensed to 1-2 sentences or moved to an appendix. -  Table 5 (model-as-facet) shows "---" for MATH precision entries.  If precision was not tested on MATH (only BF16/FP16), this should be noted explicitly rather than with a dash. 8. Questions for Authors 1.  How are negative variance component estimates handled?  Henderson Method III can produce negative estimates for near-zero components. Are these set to zero, left negative, or redistributed? This affects the separability claim. 2.  What justifies treating temperature (2-3 levels) as a random rather than fixed facet?  With 3 specific design points, the random-effects assumption is questionable. Have you compared results with temperature as fixed? 3.  For the cross-benchmark comparison, have you re-analyzed MMLU restricted to BF16/FP16 only (excluding FP32)?  This would make the precision facet comparable across benchmarks and test whether the precision gradient survives. 4.  How were the "optimal" prompt and seed counts in the D-study determined?  Is there a formal optimization procedure, or were these chosen by inspection? 5.  The bootstrap resamples items but not conditions. Have you considered a double bootstrap (resampling both items and conditions)?  This would capture total uncertainty rather than just item-sampling uncertainty. 6.  How do you address the binary data issue in G-theory estimation?  Standard methods assume continuous responses. Have you considered generalized G-theory or a probit/logit link function approach? 7.  The paper claims "current practice G<0.25 everywhere" — what specific "current practice" configuration yields this?  Is this 1 prompt × 1 seed × 200 items × 1 temperature × 1 precision? The baseline should be precisely defined. 8.  For GSM8K and MATH, how were answers extracted from generated text?  The extraction method is a potential confound for binary scoring. 9.  Were the 6 prompt templates the same across all 5 benchmarks?  If so, were they designed for MC format specifically, and how appropriate are they for GSM8K/MATH generation tasks? 10.  The fine-tuning experiment uses item-level accuracy across test set items as the response variable, or run-level aggregate accuracy?  If aggregate, G-theory is applied to a single number per run (N=432), which is a very different statistical regime than item-level analysis (N=432×test_ items). 9. Minor Issues -  The G-theory formula in Eq. 2 uses subscript notation that conflates "conditions" into a single $c$ — for a 5-facet design, the full formula should be shown or a reference to the exact formula used should be provided. -  Table 6 (cross-benchmark) reports 384,000 obs for GSM8K/ARC/HellaSwag but the experimental design (4 models × 2 prec × 6 prompts × 6 seeds × 2 temps × 4 orderings × 200 items) yields 4×2×6×6×2×4×200 = 230,400. The 384,000 figure is inconsistent — please verify. -  The paper switches between "Henderson Method I" (Section 4.6) and "Henderson Method III" (summary). These are different methods — please clarify which was used. -  Several tables show components that do not sum to 100% without explanation. A footnote about rounding and/or the treatment of negative estimates would help. -  The Related Work paragraph on training instability cites Dodge et al. (2020) but the bibliography entry has no venue information beyond "arXiv preprint." -  The Lu et al. (2022) citation appears to be incorrect — the cited paper is about emergent abilities, not option ordering. Verify this reference. -  The Mesting (2026) bibliography entry says "ACL" but the literature map says "arXiv." Verify the venue. 10. Score and Confidence Overall Score: 4/6 (Weak Accept) Confidence: High Justification The paper has substantially improved since Dream #1 by: (a) treating model as a crossed facet, (b) adding bootstrap CIs, (c) expanding to 5 benchmarks with a coherent three-tier narrative, (d) reframing infrastructure separability as confirmatory, (e) expanding the bibliography to 18 references (still below the 25+ target but much improved), and (f) acknowledging item dominance as psychometrically expected while emphasizing the benchmark-conditional gradient as the novel contribution. The cross-benchmark variance gradient — the central claim — is well-supported by data across five benchmarks, with honest uncertainty quantification (permutation p=0.003, directional not magnitude claims). The D-study reproducibility budgets fill a genuine practical gap. The metric-conditional finding (G=0.37 vs. G=0.97) is striking and immediately useful. The paper falls short of a clear accept (5/6) due to: (a) binary data in standard G-theory without discussion of the methodological limitation, (b) temperature/ordering as random facets with 2-4 levels is dubious, (c) asymmetric designs across benchmarks confound the cross-benchmark comparison of precision effects, and (d) the separability claim is overstated in the abstract given that 2/5 benchmarks show >2% infra×method interaction. These issues are addressable in revision: -  Add a paragraph discussing binary data limitations and cite generalized G-theory -  Present a sensitivity analysis with temperature as fixed -  Re-analyze MMLU at BF16/FP16 only for the cross-benchmark precision comparison -  Qualify the separability claim in the abstract with "on knowledge benchmarks" If these revisions are made, the paper would be a solid accept (5/6). The experimental scale, honest framing, and actionable D-study budgets make this a useful contribution to the evaluation methodology literature.
